text: Given an integer n, return the least number of perfect squares — one, four, nine, sixteen, and so on — that sum to n.

Thanks. Before I dive in, I'd like to clarify a few things. Just to make sure I'm understanding this correctly — I can reuse a square any number of times, and I want the minimum count. So this is really a fewest-coins problem where the coins are the perfect squares?
Exactly. n is up to ten to the fourth.
Let me run through an example. Twelve is four plus four plus four, so the answer is three. Thirteen is four plus nine, so the answer is two.

Hmm, let me think about this for a second. A naive approach would recursively try every square at every step, which repeats the same remainders over and over and blows up exponentially. This problem reminds me of unbounded knapsack where we minimize the count: the items are the squares, and each can be used any number of times. So dp of i is the fewest squares summing to i, and dp of i is the minimum over j of dp of i minus j squared, plus one. I can also view it as a BFS shortest path from zero to n, where each edge adds a square.

Here's the plan. One: set dp of zero to zero and everything else to infinity. Two: for each i from one to n, try every square j squared that fits in i. Three: take the minimum of dp of i minus j squared, plus one, then return dp of n. One thing worth flagging — a type note. Because the aggregate is a min, not a sum, the values never grow: dp of i is at most i, and by Lagrange's four-square theorem it's actually at most four. So a plain int is fine here, with no overflow worry like a counting DP has. Does this approach sound good, or would you rather I think of another way?
Sounds good. Code the DP and the BFS.

The DP fills dp from one up to n, and for each i tries every square up to i. The line that's easy to get wrong is the guard: the table starts at INT_MAX, and INT_MAX plus one would overflow, so I only relax from entries that are already finite. And the BFS is a shortest path from zero to n, where each edge adds a square. Both are n times root n. One thing worth flagging — BFS returns as soon as it first reaches n, and since all edges cost one, that first hit is the minimum.

Let's dry-run the DP on twelve, with squares one, four, and nine. The row that matters is twelve itself: from eleven it costs four, from eight it costs three, from three it costs four. The minimum is three, which is four plus four plus four. That matches. As an overflow-free check, nine thousand nine hundred ninety-nine gives four, and ten thousand gives one; the values stay tiny, so int never overflows. Corner cases: n of one is one. Seven needs four squares, the most possible.

Let me think about complexity here. Time is n times root n, and space is linear. Oh, one more thing — two notes. This is the fewest-coins problem with square coins, and because it's a min, the loop order doesn't matter and int can't overflow — unlike counting the ways, where loop order picks permutations versus combinations and the sums can overflow. And by Lagrange the answer is always one to four, so with Legendre's three-square theorem there's a root-n pure-math solution — useful if n were huge.

Nicely done. Three things stood out. You mapped it straight onto fewest coins with square coins. You reasoned that a min DP can't overflow, so int suffices, contrasting the counting case. And you brought up the BFS view and the Lagrange and Legendre root-n shortcut. Good work.
